name: Automated Testing

claims.claim_text: Once a factory's automated test equipment is fully depreciated, the marginal cost of testing each unit falls close to zero and the binding constraint on test capacity becomes tester uptime rather than test cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: testing equipment that we've had here is paid for
claims.speaker: John Edmond
claims.episode_title: An Interview with John Edmond - Luciferous LED Lucubrator

claims.claim_text: High-volume production justifies purpose-built test automation: pogo-pin fixtures, hydraulics that push boards along a jig, and flippers that sort units into pass and fail bins. At volumes in the hundreds of thousands of units, a capital budget on the order of a couple hundred thousand dollars for the test system is defensible.
claims.quote_verbatim: you might have a couple hundred thousand dollar budget to automate the testing of these things
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Senseless Saccadic Shemozzle

claims.claim_text: Automated testing of hardware changes has a hard floor on cycle time, because each iteration requires physically building and reworking boards; firmware changes have no such floor and are the better first target for automation.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're limited as to how fast your testing cycle can be
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: A firmware test rig needs four pieces that a pure software project does not: the target hardware physically attached, a programming system, an automated tool that pulls whatever was committed to the repository, and a scripted procedure that compiles, installs and exercises the build.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to have some kind of a setup where you have the attached hardware and you have programming system and some kind of automated tool to take whatever's been committed to the repo
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: A cheap way to automate mechanical actuation, capable of powering a unit up, pressing a button several hundred times and powering it back down, covers both endurance testing and design experiments such as qualifying a cross-referenced or second-source part before it enters the line.
claims.quote_verbatim: turn the machine on and press this button 500 times and then turn it off
claims.speaker: Adam Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Adam Wolf - Brick & Board Biuners

claims.claim_text: Fitting each board with a unique laser-programmed identity chip lets automated test software read the serial number and file a test report against that specific unit, which turns the test database into a troubleshooting resource for returns years later.
claims.quote_verbatim: each board has its own ID and you have automated software which reads that and then you can associate a test report with that individual board
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Motors And Upgrading Sinclairs - Adapting Apraxiated Automobiles

claims.claim_text: Connector life can be characterised with an automated insertion jig that mates and unmates a sample a thousand times at varying approach angles while the operator measures gold plating wear and predicts service life.
claims.quote_verbatim: we designed automated insertion testing jigs. So, it would make these connectors a thousand times at different angles
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: A 2013 Recap - Year-end Yarn Yakking

claims.claim_text: A second-source part built to be as close a copy as physically possible still behaves differently in endurance test, so a copied connector must be fully re-characterised and re-tested rather than assumed equivalent to the original.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's never an exact duplicate
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: A 2013 Recap - Year-end Yarn Yakking

claims.claim_text: Designing a card edge connector into the edge of the production panel makes an entire panel of boards, ten at a time, accessible to a single test fixture without individual handling.
claims.quote_verbatim: I designed in like a card edge connector on the side of the panel
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Manufacturing By Wire And Skipping Testing - Calefacient Cuculine Cash

claims.claim_text: Building an automated pass-fail jig costs a couple of weeks of design plus an open-ended debugging tail, and at low production volume that effort is not recovered; the decision to skip automation gets worse still when the fixture must be shipped to a remote assembler who will need troubleshooting guides for it.
claims.quote_verbatim: I don't really have the volume to warrant, you know, spending a couple of weeks designing that
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Manufacturing By Wire And Skipping Testing - Calefacient Cuculine Cash

claims.claim_text: Production test can be scoped as a spot-value verification against specification at a single operating point rather than a sweep across the full range, which is far cheaper than calibration; calibration exists to correct nonlinearities in precision instruments and brings a large maintenance burden with it.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's not like over the full range. It's like a spot value
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Manufacturing By Wire And Skipping Testing - Calefacient Cuculine Cash

claims.claim_text: The target state for manufacturing test instrumentation is full scriptability: probes land on the unit, the instrument walks a scripted test sequence and returns a pass-fail result without operator judgment, which also allows scopes and function generators to be tied into a pogo-pin fixture.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can just have it and, you know, like put the probes on, it'll go through whatever the test sequence is and then give you a pass fail
claims.speaker: Akiba
claims.episode_title: The Internet of Septage (with Akiba)

claims.claim_text: Production test and design verification answer different questions. Once a design is qualified, the automated test on the line is checking the assembly of that individual unit, so the failure modes it must catch are the ones introduced during build rather than the ones inherent to the schematic.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're no longer testing the design. You're testing the assembly of that particular unit
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An interview with Alvaro and Jen from the URE Podcast

claims.claim_text: Test coverage strategy differs sharply by industry: a large-scale consumer product typically ships with only a built-in self test and no calibration step, whereas at a test-equipment maker the calibration setup is one of the largest pieces of the production test system.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's not going to get, it's not doing full calibration
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Huggins

claims.claim_text: Some test scenarios can only be run by a machine because their duration makes them unsafe or unlawful for a person: one automotive customer wanted a twelve-hour overnight run that repeatedly navigated into and out of screens hoping to trigger a buffer overflow.
claims.quote_verbatim: they had a particular test scenario where they wanted it to run, uh, 12 hours, like overnight
claims.speaker: Jason Huggins
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Huggins

claims.claim_text: Teams routinely hold a list of scenarios they label untestable, and these tend to involve breaking a physical or wireless link, for example a device losing its Bluetooth connection to a phone, where no rig exists to force the disconnect on demand.
claims.quote_verbatim: we don't have an automated test for that
claims.speaker: Jason Huggins
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Huggins

claims.claim_text: The person who acquires test automation is usually not the engineer who will write the tests but that engineer's manager, because the purchase and the search for a vendor happen a level above the bench.
claims.quote_verbatim: usually it's not the end line engineer writing the test. It's their boss
claims.speaker: Jason Huggins
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Huggins

claims.claim_text: Buying a test robot does not remove the engineering labour: a skilled engineer must still consume the robot's API and author the automated tests, so the capability remains labour-intensive even when the mechanism is off the shelf.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have this robot that can click buttons on a phone, but you still need a skilled engineer to figure out how to consume that API
claims.speaker: Jason Huggins
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Huggins

claims.claim_text: Test-automation service packages priced as a fraction of an engineer's salary land in the tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars, which lets a small vendor stay profitable on engineering services rather than scaling to thousands of units of hardware.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you start talking in terms of fractions of a person's salary, you quickly get into tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of dollars
claims.speaker: Jason Huggins
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jason Huggins

claims.claim_text: Vendor FPGA toolchains resist test automation in two specific ways: they are GUI-driven rather than scriptable, and even free licences are node-locked to a MAC address, which blocks packaging the toolchain into a portable container image for automated builds and tests.
claims.quote_verbatim: even if it's a free license, it's still locked to a particular MAC address
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski
claims.episode_title: Open FPGA Toolchains at 35c3

claims.claim_text: Production volume sets the test-time budget directly: building five million greeting-card sound modules in three months leaves only seconds per unit, which forces automation regardless of how simple the device is.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you want to make 5 million cards in three months, you have to be able to test them very quickly
claims.speaker: Julia Truchsess
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Julia Truchsess

claims.claim_text: A single high-speed production tester can cover both digital and analog acceptance in one insertion, verifying the entire ROM contents of a chip alongside standby current, operating current and output drive, in roughly eight to ten seconds per unit.
claims.quote_verbatim: this tester could test the entire ROM contents of the chip as well as all the analog parameters of it, standby current, operating current, output drive
claims.speaker: Julia Truchsess
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Julia Truchsess

claims.claim_text: USB is a poor transport for sensors on a mobile robot because of connector and cabling reliability, but it is well suited to bench-side automated testing of embedded electronics, where the hub sits inside an existing enclosure and is opened and rewired by technicians.
claims.quote_verbatim: USB is not appropriate for mobile robots. Um, but it's great for many other things, including automated testing of embedded electronics
claims.speaker: Chris Osterwood
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Osterwood

claims.claim_text: Per-port current monitoring in a test hub converts a silent bus collapse into a diagnosable event: a sensor that previously drew a hundred milliamps and now draws an amp indicates a cable short, and that port can be switched off before the whole USB bus goes down.
claims.quote_verbatim: the sensor that was drawing a hundred milliamps is now drawing an amp
claims.speaker: Chris Osterwood
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Osterwood

claims.claim_text: Designing a factory programming and bus tool to be driven either from a Python library or from plain ASCII commands over a serial port keeps it usable from MATLAB, LabVIEW, Python, a Linux single-board computer on the floor, a Windows laptop or a Mac, rather than binding the test system to one language and operating system.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can access your I squared C or spy bus from any automated language that you've got from any computer
claims.speaker: Jonathan Georgino
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jonathan Georgino

claims.claim_text: Earlier factory tools exposed APIs only as a DLL that had to be linked, which pinned the whole test station to Windows, or offered access only from C; that coupling is what makes a text-protocol interface valuable in a test rig expected to last years.
claims.quote_verbatim: you almost were limited to, you need to, you know, be able to, uh, link into some DLL
claims.speaker: Jonathan Georgino
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jonathan Georgino

claims.claim_text: Automating hardware test is harder to specify than automating software test because the pass criteria depend on real-world physical characteristics that are difficult to measure, and asserting them requires test stands and instruments rather than an assertion in code.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a lot less well-defined than it might be in a software world because it might, it might involve some real world characteristics that are tough to measure
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Hardware Revision Control with Kyle Dumont

claims.claim_text: A working hardware-in-the-loop setup at a 3D printer company had the build server push each new firmware version to the machine and run a unit test suite that jogged the printer to every coordinate to confirm no axis crashed.
claims.quote_verbatim: it run through a whole series of unit tests on the printer would go like jog it to all the coordinates and make sure it didn't crash
claims.speaker: Kyle Dumont
claims.episode_title: Hardware Revision Control with Kyle Dumont

claims.claim_text: Attaching a regression test to the change that fixes a defect means the condition is re-checked on every future version, so the test suite accumulates protection against exactly the failures the product has already exhibited.
claims.quote_verbatim: it will be tested at each future version to make sure that, um, it doesn't fail those conditions
claims.speaker: Kyle Dumont
claims.episode_title: Hardware Revision Control with Kyle Dumont

claims.claim_text: Renode, an open-source embedded systems simulator that has existed in some form since 2010, lets a team execute tests and gather metrics against a simulated target, removing physical hardware from the loop for the bulk of test runs.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can also use the software, execute tests, gather metrics without touching hardware
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Simulating Embedded Hardware with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Whether a board gets manual or automated test is decided by volume: low-volume boards are tested by hand, and the same board moves to an automated fixture once volume rises.
claims.quote_verbatim: for our pcbs we are setting up test gigs that do automated testing or depending on the volume
claims.speaker: Fredrik Kensander
claims.episode_title: High Current Power Supplies with Fredrik Kensander

claims.claim_text: One workable division of labour with a contract manufacturer is for the product owner to design and build the test stand in-house and ship it to the assembler, who then runs it as incoming acceptance test on every board.
claims.quote_verbatim: a test stand and send it to them so they run it
claims.speaker: Fredrik Kensander
claims.episode_title: High Current Power Supplies with Fredrik Kensander

claims.claim_text: Staged automated test at each level of assembly keeps fault-finding cheap: at the contract manufacturer a mini variant of the power module board is driven from a 24 volt AC input while its switching pulses are measured, then the assembled module goes through an automated module tester, and only then is it built into a stack.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have a 24 volt AC input to that board and it's switching and then we're measuring and making sure everything works that the pulses are correct
claims.speaker: Fredrik Kensander
claims.episode_title: High Current Power Supplies with Fredrik Kensander

claims.claim_text: Final system test can remain automated in its measurement while still needing an operator, because connecting many cables and the cooling water for a water-cooled stack cannot be automated economically.
claims.quote_verbatim: the final testing which also an automated test but with personal because you need to connect a lot of cables and the cooling water
claims.speaker: Fredrik Kensander
claims.episode_title: High Current Power Supplies with Fredrik Kensander

claims.claim_text: When every subassembly has already passed its own automated test, the final system test should pass without incident; a final test that regularly finds faults is evidence that coverage is missing further upstream.
claims.quote_verbatim: pass without problems because yeah each individual piece is good
claims.speaker: Fredrik Kensander
claims.episode_title: High Current Power Supplies with Fredrik Kensander

claims.claim_text: The test instrument industry is historically closed, and its established control standards, SCPI over GPIB and the later LXI, were designed for command-and-response measurement rather than for streaming data, which is why they perform poorly when a test script needs a continuous sample stream.
claims.quote_verbatim: The test instrument industry is often very closed
claims.speaker: Matt Liberty
claims.episode_title: Measuring Current with Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: The economic case for scripting a bench procedure is that writing the script takes roughly the same time as performing the procedure once by hand, after which it can be repeated indefinitely in the identical order, which matters for calibration and any sequence whose validity depends on ordering.
claims.quote_verbatim: why do that when you can write a script in, you know, the same time that it would take, and now you can run it all the time?
claims.speaker: Matt Liberty
claims.episode_title: Measuring Current with Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: A fully automated board line can chain surface mount, depanel, jig loading, electrical test and packaging with no manual handling, though even a mature high-volume operation may still have people loading parts into test sockets while the last robot cell is brought online.
claims.quote_verbatim: put in a jig by robots, tested by robots, packaged by robots
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: Embedded Hardware with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: Manual RF characterisation that required roughly 900 connector matings was reduced to about 30 connections by an automated switching system, a factor of a hundred fewer, which also removed the repetitive strain injury risk from screwing precision connectors on and off.
claims.quote_verbatim: we developed a system that could knock that down by like a factor of 100. So they could do like, you know, 30 connections instead of 900 connections
claims.speaker: Joel Dunsmore
claims.episode_title: Microwave measurement with Joel Dunsmore

claims.claim_text: Standing up a remote hardware test setup once is straightforward; keeping it available to a whole team indefinitely is a different and much harder class of problem, and that operational burden is the real cost of hardware test infrastructure.
claims.quote_verbatim: getting it working one day is fine. And getting it working for your whole team forever is like a whole different class of problem
claims.speaker: Akbar Dhanaliwala
claims.episode_title: Firmware Deployment and Troubleshooting with Akbar Dhanaliwala

claims.claim_text: A large software product's daily build was gated by a large body of automated test scripts, and a build's automated results were used as a triage filter: if a build failed enough of them, engineers would not spend time testing it manually at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: there was also automated testing as well. They had countless automated testing scripts
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Works on my machine

claims.claim_text: Because the unit is already electrically accessible in the end-of-line jig at the moment of programming, that is the cheapest point to do everything else to it and emit one consolidated test report for that specific serial number, rather than splitting programming and test across separate stations and vendors.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a great time to pretty much do everything you can to it and have a fully integrated test report for that specific unit
claims.speaker: Pete Staples
claims.episode_title: Standardizing Manufacturing with Pete Staples

claims.claim_text: A general end-of-line test instrument needs a command-and-measure loop over UART, CAN bus stimulus, voltage, current and resistance measurement and a frequency counter, since those cover the interactions most projects actually require at the end of the line.
claims.quote_verbatim: Voltage, current, resistance measurements, there's a frequency counter.
claims.speaker: Pete Staples
claims.episode_title: Standardizing Manufacturing with Pete Staples

claims.claim_text: Running the same C test suite twice, once compiled for x86 on the development machine and once cross-compiled and executed on the target, uses the second run purely as a cross-check that the port itself succeeded, since porting reliably introduces its own defects.
claims.quote_verbatim: run the same set of tests on the hardware, just as a good cross check. Like did my porting succeed?
claims.speaker: Phillip Johnston
claims.episode_title: Firmware for Hardware Engineers with Phillip Johnston

claims.claim_text: Manual test procedures are not actually executed on every build: engineers forget, run out of time, or decide an item is not worth checking, so a manual regression plan silently decays while an automated one does not.
claims.quote_verbatim: in a manual process, that's just not going to happen. It's not feasible. You forget, you don't have the time.
claims.speaker: Phillip Johnston
claims.episode_title: Firmware for Hardware Engineers with Phillip Johnston

claims.claim_text: A system that was not architected for testability can feel impossible to bring under test later, because the hardware dependencies are tangled through the code and prevent any part of it from running on a development machine.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you didn't design your system in a particular way at the start, it can feel impossible to, to bring it under test
claims.speaker: Phillip Johnston
claims.episode_title: Firmware for Hardware Engineers with Phillip Johnston

claims.claim_text: A low-effort entry point to firmware test automation is to exercise the serial or USB command line that most embedded projects already have: a Python script opens the serial connection, issues commands and checks for the expected responses from the device.
claims.quote_verbatim: have a Python script that opens up a serial connection and start sending commands and checking for expected responses on the device
claims.speaker: Phillip Johnston
claims.episode_title: Firmware for Hardware Engineers with Phillip Johnston

claims.claim_text: The gap between hardware and software change review is functional confirmation: nothing automatically tells a reviewer that a changed feedback resistor still behaves as intended, whereas software review has cheap access to test frameworks that answer that question.
claims.quote_verbatim: a reviewer functionally confirm that the resistor change is working as expected
claims.speaker: Michael Corr
claims.episode_title: Product Lifecycle Management with Michael Corr

claims.claim_text: Treating test data as first-class product data means designing instrumentation into the firmware rather than hanging a UART-to-USB adapter on the board and printing at the first bug, because the ad hoc route yields data no automated test can consume.
claims.quote_verbatim: your UART to USB adapter on there and print out some stuff on your UART
claims.speaker: Charles Aylward
claims.episode_title: Software for Rockets with Charles Aylward

claims.claim_text: Bed-of-nails fixtures can themselves cause the defect they fail to detect: pogo pin pressure flexes the board, and the crack in a ceramic capacitor forms as the pins lift and the board springs back, after the measurement has already been taken.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you lift the pins back off, that's actually, you know, the board flexes back and that's what does the cracking
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Return of the Trade Show Jedi

claims.claim_text: A board damaged by its own test fixture ships as fully tested and then exhibits a long-term failure in the field, sometimes only appearing with temperature, mechanical stress, or when the unit is screwed down at its mounting points.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's cracked or it has a long-term failure mode
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Return of the Trade Show Jedi

claims.claim_text: Firmware automated testing is rare in practice because setting it up against real hardware is complicated, which is the gap that device simulation targets.
claims.quote_verbatim: I know most people just don't do it because it's pretty complicated to do with real hardware
claims.speaker: Uri Shaked
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Uri Shaked (Wokwi.com)

claims.claim_text: Running each new build against a simulated device rather than physical hardware covers most of the behaviour of interest and is a reasonable gate before promoting a build to a real integration-level test on hardware.
claims.quote_verbatim: that might get you 98% of the way there
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Uri Shaked (Wokwi.com)

claims.claim_text: Tuning a few firmware constants against environmental variation required physically carrying the device to different rooms and returning at different times of day, a manual matrix that simulation collapses into repeatable automated runs.
claims.quote_verbatim: all I wanted to do was just tweak a few numbers in the firmware to find a combination that works best in all the scenarios
claims.speaker: Uri Shaked
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Uri Shaked (Wokwi.com)

claims.claim_text: Running a physical test sequence once or twice by hand is acceptable, but repeating it introduces human error into the results, which makes repeated manual verification the natural first candidate for automation.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's human error that like comes into there. So like, this is just a perfect place for automation.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Uri Shaked (Wokwi.com)

claims.claim_text: In a hardware-in-the-loop flow, a precision current measurement instrument can be folded into the same run that executes the functional tests, so current and energy consumption are recorded as a tracked metric over time rather than measured only when someone suspects a problem.
claims.quote_verbatim: you push up your changes, you run whatever tests you would normally run, and as part of that, you also measure your current or energy consumption
claims.speaker: Matt Liberty
claims.episode_title: The Joulescope Upgrade with Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: Exhaustive testing of a configurable instrument is physically impossible, because the number of permutations of settings grows far faster than any test budget; coverage decisions therefore have to select which configurations matter rather than aiming for completeness.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't run it through every test, every permutation. You can't, you physically can't do it.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Super Tecmo Bug

claims.claim_text: Configuration-dependent performance regressions are a real failure class in instrument firmware: enabling a single horizontal measurement on an oscilloscope dropped waveform processing and update rate by about three orders of magnitude, a defect invisible to any test that does not exercise that specific combination.
claims.quote_verbatim: causes like three orders of magnitude drop in update in waveform processing and update rate speed
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Super Tecmo Bug

claims.claim_text: Using a company's own programmable instruments to manufacture and calibrate the next generation of those instruments tests the scripting interface in the loop, but risks generational calibration drift, so a separately traceable calibrated multimeter is placed in series as the reference.
claims.quote_verbatim: in order not to introduce generational degrade there is a least traceable calibrated multimeter in series
claims.speaker: Werner Johansson
claims.episode_title: Software Defined Power Supplies with Werner Johansson

claims.claim_text: Vacuum tube burn-in was automated with an electromechanical timer that sequenced racks and rows, holding the heaters on continuously and switching each rack under load for a measured period overnight before the tubes were pulled the next day.
claims.quote_verbatim: it would put the racks under load for a measured period of time
claims.speaker: Fran Blanche
claims.episode_title: Dave hanging with Fran Blanche

claims.claim_text: The automated tester that followed burn-in ran each tube individually through a cycle of measurements, and the resulting parameter data was used to match tubes into sets rather than only to pass or fail them.
claims.quote_verbatim: it would run each tube individually in the tester and put it through these various cycles, take measurements
claims.speaker: Fran Blanche
claims.episode_title: Dave hanging with Fran Blanche

claims.claim_text: Production test software has an extremely long service life and pins the factory to obsolete platforms: test racks built around Windows 3.1.1 were still in production use into the late 2000s.
claims.quote_verbatim: I still had production test racks running Windows 3.1.1 into the late 2000s.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Dave hanging with Fran Blanche

claims.claim_text: Moving from prototype to high-volume manufacturing has prerequisites in the board itself, since a prototype-level design cannot be run through a high-volume setup unchanged; building the test automation solution is part of that transition work.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can't have a prototype level board to be manufactured in very high volume setup.
claims.speaker: Pallav Aggarwal
claims.episode_title: Blogging Electronics with Pallav Aggarwal

claims.claim_text: Physical testing dominates development time for embedded control systems, consuming roughly 80 percent of the effort on university drone and sensor work, because each scenario requires holding hardware and mounting things in the real world.
claims.quote_verbatim: like 80% of the time was just testing
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: System Designer Lets You Try Every Part with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Field testing of a physical system is always incomplete, not because engineers lack the ability but because the effort per additional scenario is high enough that coverage stops well short of what the design warrants.
claims.quote_verbatim: you still don't test everything because you like you can't be bothered to
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: System Designer Lets You Try Every Part with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Simulated targets change the economics of coverage in two ways: additional scenarios cost only compute and parallelise across many servers, so a thousand simulation runs can execute simultaneously.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can have a thousand Renode runs across a thousand servers
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: System Designer Lets You Try Every Part with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: A simulated system that spends most of its time reading, writing and sleeping can have its time base compressed, so a week of real behaviour is exercised in about fifteen minutes; the technique breaks down when the system is busy-looping, which is hard to simulate faster than real time.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can take like a week's worth of data and compress that to, let's say, 15 minutes
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: System Designer Lets You Try Every Part with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Manufacturing test is a distinct discipline from bench test, driven largely by software and instrument drivers, and its optimisation targets are throughput, test time per unit, and deciding how much really needs to be tested at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: They're concerned about throughput and, you know, how quickly can I test this and how much do I really need to test
claims.speaker: Martin Rowe
claims.episode_title: The Measurement Blues with Martin Rowe

Passage 21 is flagged ATTRIB-UNRELIABLE but the content is the guest describing his own USB hub product; attributed to Chris Osterwood.
